proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an accepted input \(\mathfrak u\), a table \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\), and a graph \(D\in\mathfrak D\).  Write \(\operatorname{CI}(D)\) for the elementary conditional-independence statements implied by d-separation in \(D\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}sparsest\text{-}dag\text{-}family}\), retention of \(D\) means precisely that
\[
 \operatorname{CI}(D)\subseteq\{c:\mathcal I(c)=1\}. \tag{1}
\]
For every statement \(c\) in the set on the right, \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}oracle\text{-}model}\) and the oracle-one condition say that every determinantal minor encoding \(c\) vanishes at \(p\).  Thus every member of \(\operatorname{CI}(D)\) holds under \(p\).  This is the global Markov property of \(p\) with respect to \(D\).  Since \(D\) was arbitrary,
\[
 \mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}
 \subseteq\bigcap_{D\in\mathfrak D}\mathcal M(D), \tag{2}
\]
where \(\mathcal M(D)\) is the set of probability laws globally Markov to \(D\).  Intersecting both sides of (2) with \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\) gives
\[
 \mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\cap
 \bigcap_{D\in\mathfrak D}\mathcal M(D)
 =\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}. \tag{3}
\]

Finally, a graph-local Markov determinantal generator for \(D\) encodes a statement in \(\operatorname{CI}(D)\).  By (1), that statement has oracle bit one, and by the definition of \(\mathcal C_1(\mathcal I)\), the same minor is already a generator of
\[
 J_{\mathcal I}
 =\left\langle\mathcal C_1(\mathcal I),
       \sum_{z\in\Omega}p_z-1\right\rangle. \tag{4}
\]
Consequently adjoining graph-local Markov minors changes neither this ideal nor its zero set on the declared exact-oracle domain.  Equations (2)--(4) prove all assertions.

Put \(R_0=\mathbb Q[p_z:z\in\Omega]\) and \(L=J_{\mathcal I}:s^{\infty}\), and fix \(D\in\mathfrak D\) and an outcome cell \(y\).  The defining property of reduction by the canonical reduced basis is
\[
 \operatorname{NF}_{\prec,K_{\mathcal I}}(F_{D,y})=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_{D,y}\in K_{\mathcal I}. \tag{5}
\]
By \(\mathrm{def{:}saturated\text{-}real\text{-}radical}\), the right side of (5) says that \(F_{D,y}\) vanishes on the real variety of \(L\).  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}real\text{-}nullstellensatz}\) after scalar extension to \(\mathbb R\).  There are an integer \(a\geq1\), finitely many \(q_i\in\mathbb R[p_z:z\in\Omega]\), and an element \(h\in L\mathbb R[p_z:z\in\Omega]\) such that
\[
 F_{D,y}^{\,2a}+\sum_iq_i^2=h. \tag{6}
\]
Ideal membership in (6) has a finite representation
\[
 h=\sum_{\nu=1}^k b_\nu\ell_\nu,
 \qquad
 b_\nu\in\mathbb R[p_z:z\in\Omega],
 \quad \ell_\nu\in L. \tag{7}
\]
For every \(\nu\), the definition of saturation supplies \(N_\nu\geq0\) with \(s^{N_\nu}\ell_\nu\in J_{\mathcal I}\).  Taking \(N=\max_\nu N_\nu\) and multiplying (6) by \(s^N\) therefore yields membership in the explicitly finitely generated ideal \(J_{\mathcal I}\mathbb R[p_z:z\in\Omega]\).  If \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) are its rational generators, there are \(a_j\in\mathbb R[p_z:z\in\Omega]\) for which
\[
 s^N\left(F_{D,y}^{\,2a}+\sum_iq_i^2\right)
   =\sum_{j=1}^r a_jf_j. \tag{8}
\]

Fix the integers \(a,N,k,r\) and all finite monomial supports occurring in one solution of (8).  Equating coefficients in (8) is then a finite existential sentence in the unknown coefficients of the \(q_i\) and \(a_j\), with rational coefficients.  It is true in \(\mathbb R\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}real\text{-}closed\text{-}field\text{-}transfer}\), it is true in the real algebraic closure \(\mathbb R_{\mathrm{alg}}\) of \(\mathbb Q\).  Thus all coefficients in (8) may be chosen in \(\mathbb R_{\mathrm{alg}}\).  The finitely many coefficients generate a finite real algebraic extension \(E/\mathbb Q\).

Identity (8) is both the real-Nullstellensatz and saturation certificate.  Indeed, let \(r\) be a real point at which every generator of \(J_{\mathcal I}\) vanishes and \(s(r)\neq0\).  Evaluating (8) and dividing by \(s(r)^N\), which is permitted by the displayed nonvanishing condition, gives
\[
 F_{D,y}(r)^{2a}+\sum_iq_i(r)^2=0. \tag{9}
\]
All summands in (9) are nonnegative in the selected real embedding of \(E\), so \(F_{D,y}(r)=0\).  This is exactly the advertised vanishing consequence.

It remains to account for verification size.  Encode \(E\) by a primitive element, its square-free defining polynomial, and rational isolating or Thom data for the selected real root; encode every coefficient in the power basis.  The certificate also supplies every polynomial and every product in (8) in expanded form.  A checker uses exact rational polynomial arithmetic to verify the algebraic-number representation, reduces coefficient products modulo the defining polynomial, recomputes the advertised polynomial products, and compares the two expanded coefficient maps.  If \(L_{\mathrm{cert}}\) is the total expanded input length, the number of coefficient operations is bounded by a quadratic polynomial in \(L_{\mathrm{cert}}\); unary exponents ensure that repeated powering requires at most \(L_{\mathrm{cert}}\) advertised multiplications, and the bit lengths of sums and products are polynomial in the total bit length of their supplied operands.  Sturm or subresultant sign checks for the isolating data are likewise polynomial in the displayed degrees and coefficient bit lengths.  Hence deterministic exact verification is polynomial in \(L_{\mathrm{cert}}\).  This is a verifier bound only; the argument asserts no uniform bound on the shortest certificate or on the time needed to find it.

Fix a finite syntactically certified input \(\mathfrak u\).  We prove the three-way termination statement, exactness of the quotient, the certificate claims, the decision counts, and finally the causal interpretation.

For each oracle-zero conditional-independence statement \(c\), define
\[
 h_c(p)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal C_0(\mathcal I,c)}g(p)^2,
\]
and form the finite rational polynomial sets
\[
 E_0=\mathcal C_1(\mathcal I)\cup
 \left\{\sum_{z\in\Omega}p_z-1\right\},
 \qquad
 G_0=H_0=\{p_z:z\in\Omega\}
       \cup\{h_c:\mathcal I(c)=0\}. \tag{10}
\]
In the notation of \(\mathrm{lem{:}semialgebraic\text{-}decision\text{-}with\text{-}certificates}\), the equality
\[
 S(E_0,G_0,H_0)=\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ} \tag{11}
\]
is exact.  Indeed, \(p_z\geq0\) and \(p_z\neq0\) are jointly equivalent to \(p_z>0\), while each \(h_c\) is a sum of squares, so \(h_c\geq0\) and \(h_c\neq0\) are jointly equivalent to \(h_c>0\).  The equalities in \(E_0\) are precisely normalization and all oracle-one minors.  Thus (11) follows from \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}oracle\text{-}model}\).

The cited semialgebraic decision lemma decides emptiness in (11) after finitely many exact operations.  If (11) is empty, its finite quantifier-elimination trace or Positivstellensatz identity proves alternative (i).  If it is nonempty, the same lemma returns an exactly encoded point in
\[
 \mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\cap\mathbb R_{\mathrm{alg}}^\Omega. \tag{12}
\]
A supplied rational table \(p^{\circ}\) replaces (12) only after exact verification of all conditions in (11).  Hence no rational-realizability assumption has entered the domain.

We next construct the graph family.  There are only finitely many directed graphs on \(V\).  More explicitly, every DAG occurs among the at most
\[
 q!\,2^{\binom q2} \tag{13}
\]
pairs consisting of a topological order and a subset of its forward pairs.  After deduplication, acyclicity, compliance with every required or forbidden orientation in \(\mathcal B\), and d-separation are finite combinatorial tests.  Since \(\mathcal I\) is a complete bit-vector, the I-map condition is exactly
\[
 \operatorname{CI}(D)\subseteq\{c:\mathcal I(c)=1\}. \tag{14}
\]
Comparing the finitely many edge counts retains all and only the minimum-edge ties.  If no graph passes, listing each candidate together with a cycle, a background violation, or a d-separation whose oracle bit is zero is a finite exhaustive rejection certificate, proving alternative (ii).  A supplied \(\mathfrak G\) may replace this enumeration only after its certificates prove that its expansion is exactly the same retained set.  Formula (13) is solely a finiteness bound and makes no favorable complexity assertion.

Assume now that both \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\) and \(\mathfrak D\) are nonempty.  Put
\[
 \mathcal Y=\prod_{v\in Y}\Omega_v,
 \qquad N_Y=|\mathcal Y|<\infty, \tag{15}
\]
and fix the prescribed cell \(y_\star\in\mathcal Y\).  The finite marginalizations and rational reductions in \(\mathrm{def{:}truncated\text{-}functional}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}pairwise\text{-}cross\text{-}signature}\) construct every \(T_{D,y}=A_{D,y}/B_{D,y}\) and every \(F_{D,D',y}\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}truncated\text{-}vector\text{-}normalization}\), for all \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\),
\[
 B_{D,y}(p)B_{D',y}(p)>0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}T_{D,y}(p)
 =\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}T_{D',y}(p)=1. \tag{16}
\]

For an unordered pair \(\{D,D'\}\) and a cell \(y\neq y_\star\), let
\[
 H_{D,D',y}=H_0\cup\{F_{D,D',y}\}. \tag{17}
\]
Equations (11) and (17) give
\[
 S(E_0,G_0,H_{D,D',y})
 =\{p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}:
       F_{D,D',y}(p)\neq0\}. \tag{18}
\]
On the domain in (18), positivity of the denominators in (16) and \(\mathrm{def{:}pairwise\text{-}cross\text{-}signature}\) yield the equivalence
\[
 F_{D,D',y}(p)\neq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T_{D,y}(p)\neq T_{D',y}(p). \tag{19}
\]

Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}semialgebraic\text{-}decision\text{-}with\text{-}certificates}\) to (18).  If it is feasible, the algorithm returns an exactly checkable point
\[
 p^\dagger\in
 \mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\cap\mathbb R_{\mathrm{alg}}^\Omega,
 \qquad
 T_{D,y}(p^\dagger)\neq T_{D',y}(p^\dagger), \tag{20}
\]
with rational-univariate, minimal-polynomial, and isolating or Thom data.  If (18) is infeasible, its quantifier-elimination trace or Positivstellensatz identity proves that the two coordinates agree everywhere on \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\).  Before that call, a zero fixed-order normal form may replace it by \(\mathrm{lem{:}pairwise\text{-}zero\text{-}normal\text{-}form\text{-}soundness}\).  A nonzero normal form is not used as a separation conclusion.  Direct exact evaluation at the retained sample in (12), or at a verified optional \(p^{\circ}\), is also a sound feasible fast path.

If every tested coordinate for \(\{D,D'\}\) is universally equal, normalization in (16) gives, for every \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\),
\[
 T_{D,y_\star}(p)-T_{D',y_\star}(p)
 =-\sum_{y\neq y_\star}
   \{T_{D,y}(p)-T_{D',y}(p)\}=0. \tag{21}
\]
Conversely, any feasible test (20) disproves universal equality of the intervention vectors.  Therefore these decisions compute exactly the relation
\[
 D\sim D'
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T_{D,y}(p)=T_{D',y}(p)
 \text{ for every }p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}
 \text{ and every }y\in\mathcal Y. \tag{22}
\]

Relation (22) is reflexive and symmetric because equality is.  It is transitive because, pointwise in \((p,y)\),
\[
 T_{D,y}(p)=T_{D',y}(p),\quad
 T_{D',y}(p)=T_{D'',y}(p)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 T_{D,y}(p)=T_{D'',y}(p). \tag{23}
\]
Thus it is an equivalence relation.  Choose the first DAG in each class as its representative.  For every within-class graph pair, the infeasibility identity or zero-normal-form identity proves equality in each tested coordinate, and (21) proves the omitted coordinate.  For representatives of two distinct classes, the negation of (22) supplies a differing coordinate at some table.  The difference cannot occur only at \(y_\star\), by (21); hence at least one tested formula is feasible and supplies (20).  Since every graph equals its representative throughout its own class, the same table separates the corresponding members of the two classes through the representative circuits.

Let \(\Pi\) be any partition of \(\mathfrak D\) on every block of which one intervention functional is common.  Any two graphs in a block of \(\Pi\) satisfy (22), so each block of \(\Pi\) is contained in one returned class.  Thus \(\Pi\) refines the returned partition.  Conversely, (22) itself supplies one common representative functional on each returned class.  The returned quotient is therefore the unique coarsest common-functional partition.

There are \(\binom{|\mathfrak D|}{2}\) unordered graph pairs and \(N_Y-1\) tested cells for each pair.  This proves the upper bound
\[
 \binom{|\mathfrak D|}{2}(N_Y-1). \tag{24}
\]
Against one fixed reference \(D_0\), there are only \(|\mathfrak D|-1\) graph pairs, giving
\[
 (|\mathfrak D|-1)(N_Y-1). \tag{25}
\]
These counts exclude the single initial model-nonemptiness decision.  A normal-form certificate or a successful exact-sample test eliminates a semialgebraic call and therefore cannot increase either count.  Every loop is over a finite set, and every invoked exact decision procedure terminates, so the algorithm terminates.  Alternatives (i)--(iii) are mutually exclusive by their nonemptiness clauses and exhaustive by the first two decisions.

It remains to relate the observable circuits to the causal query.  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}common\text{-}law\text{-}redundancy}\), every \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\) is Markov to every \(D\in\mathfrak D\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}dag\text{-}intervention\text{-}functional}\), for each pair \((p,D)\) there is a recursive Markovian structural causal model with observed law \(p\), and every such model satisfies
\[
 P_x^D(Y=y)=T_{D,y}(p). \tag{26}
\]
If (22) has one class, (26) proves that its representative observable circuit identifies the common causal law in every represented-DAG Markovian structural causal model.  If it has more than one class, (20) and (26) construct two compatible structural causal models, one for each separated representative DAG, having the same strictly positive exact-oracle observed law \(p^\dagger\) but different intervention laws.  Thus the returned point is a causal ambiguity witness, not merely an algebraic discrepancy.  This proves every assertion of the theorem.

Write \(t=t_\star=1/3\).  Summing the unnormalised numerator of \(p_\star\) over \(s_3\) and \(s_4\) gives
\[
 \sum_{s_3=\pm1}(1+ts_1s_3)(1+ts_2s_3)
   =2(1+t^2s_1s_2),
\]
\[
 \sum_{s_4=\pm1}(1+ts_1s_4)(1-ts_2s_4)
   =2(1-t^2s_1s_2). \tag{27}
\]
Their product is \(4(1-t^4)\), independently of \((s_1,s_2)\).  Summing over the four choices of \((s_1,s_2)\) yields \(16(1-t^4)\), exactly the denominator in the definition of \(p_\star\).  Thus the table is normalized.  Every numerator factor belongs to \(\{2/3,4/3\}\), so every cell is strictly positive.  In lexicographic \((-1,+1)\) order its cells are
\[
 \frac1{40}(4,4,1,1,4,1,4,1,1,4,1,4,1,1,4,4). \tag{28}
\]
In particular the table is rational and its minimum cell is \(1/40\).

Equation (27) gives \(p_\star(s_1,s_2)=1/4\), so \(1\perp2\).  Interchanging the pairs \((s_1,s_2)\) and \((s_3,s_4)\) gives \(p_\star(s_3,s_4)=1/4\), so \(3\perp4\).  Conditional on \((s_1,s_2)\), the numerator is a product of one function of \(s_3\) and one function of \(s_4\), proving \(3\perp4\mid\{1,2\}\).  Conditional on \((s_3,s_4)\), it is a product of one function of \(s_1\) and one function of \(s_2\), proving \(1\perp2\mid\{3,4\}\).

To show that there are no further elementary independences, for distinct \(i,j\) and \(C\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}\), use the binary conditional-independence minor
\[
 \Delta_{ij\mid C}(a,b,c)
 =p(a,b,c)p(c)-p(a,c)p(b,c). \tag{29}
\]
Direct integer summation from (28) gives the following nonzero minor for each of the other twenty statements.  In every row take \(a=b=-1\), and set all displayed coordinates of \(c\) equal to \(-1\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c@{\qquad}c|c|c}
(i,j)&C&\Delta&(i,j)&C&\Delta\\ \hline
(1,2)&\{3\}&-9/1600 &(1,2)&\{4\}&9/1600\\
(1,3)&\varnothing&3/40 &(1,3)&\{2\}&3/160\\
(1,3)&\{4\}&3/160 &(1,3)&\{2,4\}&3/1600\\
(1,4)&\varnothing&3/40 &(1,4)&\{2\}&3/160\\
(1,4)&\{3\}&3/160 &(1,4)&\{2,3\}&3/400\\
(2,3)&\varnothing&3/40 &(2,3)&\{1\}&3/160\\
(2,3)&\{4\}&3/160 &(2,3)&\{1,4\}&3/400\\
(2,4)&\varnothing&-3/40 &(2,4)&\{1\}&-3/160\\
(2,4)&\{3\}&-3/160 &(2,4)&\{1,3\}&-3/400\\
(3,4)&\{1\}&-9/1600 &(3,4)&\{2\}&9/1600
\end{array} \tag{30}
\]
The four factorizations just proved make every minor for the four asserted statements vanish, whereas (30) gives a nonzero minor for every remaining elementary statement.  Hence the displayed four are exact.

We next verify the graph counts without a genericity premise.  Inclusion--exclusion on the nonempty set of sources gives the number \(a_q\) of labelled DAGs on \(q\) vertices:
\[
 a_q=\sum_{k=1}^q(-1)^{k+1}{q\choose k}
       2^{k(q-k)}a_{q-k},
 \qquad a_0=1. \tag{31}
\]
Successive substitution yields \((a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)=(1,1,3,25,543)\).

The nonzero minors in (30) show that each cross pair
\[
 \{1,3\},\ \{1,4\},\ \{2,3\},\ \{2,4\} \tag{32}
\]
is dependent given every subset of the other two vertices.  If a pair in (32) were nonadjacent in an I-map DAG, take its later endpoint in a topological order.  The earlier endpoint is then a nonparent nondescendant, so the DAG local Markov property d-separates the pair given the later endpoint's parent set, a subset of the other two vertices.  This contradicts (30).  Thus all four edges in (32) occur in every I-map, and no I-map has fewer than four edges.

At four edges the skeleton is therefore the four-cycle formed by (32).  Of its \(16\) orientations, precisely the two directed cycles are not acyclic.  Checking the collider status on the two paths between each opposite pair in the remaining \(14\) orientations gives exactly two I-maps:
\[
 \{1\to3,1\to4,2\to3,2\to4\},
 \qquad
 \{3\to1,3\to2,4\to1,4\to2\}. \tag{33}
\]
The first implies only \(1\perp2\) and \(3\perp4\mid\{1,2\}\) among nonadjacent-pair statements; the second implies only \(3\perp4\) and \(1\perp2\mid\{3,4\}\).  Every other acyclic orientation makes one opposite pair d-separated under a conditioning set ruled out by (30).  These are exactly \(D_A\) and \(D_B\).

For completeness, the higher-edge counts can also be obtained directly.  A five-edge skeleton is \(K_4\) with one missing pair.  The missing pair must be \(\{1,2\}\) or \(\{3,4\}\), since all cross pairs are forced by (32).  For \(K_4\setminus\{a,b\}\), with remaining vertices \(c,d\), its \(18\) acyclic orientations have the following exhaustive active-path classification:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\text{unique set }C\text{ with }a\mathbin{\perp_D}b\mid C
 &\varnothing&\{c\}&\{d\}&\{c,d\}\\ \hline
\text{number of orientations}&2&3&3&10.
\end{array} \tag{34}
\]
To verify (34), orient the four edges incident to \(a,b\), orient \(c-d\), discard an orientation exactly when one of the two resulting triangles is directed, and inspect the two length-two and two length-three paths from \(a\) to \(b\); these five binary arrow choices give the four displayed counts \(2,3,3,10\), summing to \(18\).  For the missing pair \(\{1,2\}\), precisely the \(2+10=12\) orientations associated with \(C=\varnothing\) or \(C=\{3,4\}\) are I-maps.  By symmetry another \(12\) arise when the missing pair is \(\{3,4\}\).  Finally, a complete four-node DAG entails no nontrivial d-separation and is automatically an I-map; there are \(4!=24\) such acyclic orientations.  Hence the exact number of I-maps is
\[
 2+12+12+24=50, \tag{35}
\]
and (33) are the unique four-edge minima.  They are in different Markov equivalence classes because \(D_A\) d-separates \(1\) and \(2\), while \(D_B\) does not, and \(D_B\) d-separates \(3\) and \(4\), while \(D_A\) does not.

The two required DAG factorizations follow from the four established conditional independences.  Under \(D_A\), truncation at \(s_1=+1\) and summation over \(s_2,s_4\) give
\[
 T_{D_A,+1}(p_\star)
 =\sum_{s_2}p_\star(s_2)
   p_\star(s_3=+1\mid s_1=+1,s_2)
 =p_\star(s_3=+1\mid s_1=+1), \tag{36}
\]
where the last equality uses \(1\perp2\).  Direct sign summation in the displayed family gives uniform one-variable marginals and
\[
 \mathbb E_{p_t}(s_1s_3)
 =\frac{t(1-t^2)}{1-t^4}
 =\frac{t}{1+t^2}. \tag{37}
\]
With \(t=1/3\), (36)--(37) imply
\[
 T_{D_A,+1}(p_\star)
 =\frac12+\frac{t}{2(1+t^2)}
 =\frac{13}{20}. \tag{38}
\]
Under \(D_B\), node \(3\) is an unmanipulated root.  Removing the factor for intervened node \(1\) and summing the other normalized kernels gives
\[
 T_{D_B,+1}(p_\star)=p_\star(s_3=+1)=\frac12. \tag{39}
\]
The factorizations just used make \(p_\star\) Markov to the respective DAGs, and strict positivity was proved from (28).  Therefore \(\mathrm{lem{:}dag\text{-}intervention\text{-}functional}\) identifies (38)--(39) with the probabilities of \(Y_3=+1\) under \(do(Y_1=+1)\), rather than merely with regression functionals.  The finite supports, disjoint query sets, empty background set, exact oracle from (29)--(30), exhaustive family from (31)--(35), and verified rational table satisfy every check in \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\text{-}input}\).  Thus \(\mathfrak u_\star\) is accepted and all claims follow.

Take \(X=\{1\}\), \(Y=\{3\}\), and \(\mathfrak G_\star=\{D_A,D_B\}\).  The first condition in \(\mathrm{lem{:}teh\text{-}sufficient\text{-}criterion}\) prohibits a proper semidirected path from \(X\) to \(Y\) beginning with an undirected edge.  Both represented graphs are DAGs, so this condition holds vacuously.

For the pairwise condition, node \(1\) is an ancestor of node \(3\) in \(D_A\), whereas it is not an ancestor of node \(3\) in \(D_B\).  Hence
\[
 A_A=X\cap\operatorname{An}_{D_A}(Y)=\{1\},
 \qquad
 A_B=X\cap\operatorname{An}_{D_B}(Y)=\varnothing. \tag{40}
\]
Every chain component of a DAG is a singleton, and the pertinent parent sets disagree:
\[
 \operatorname{pa}_{D_A}(1)=\varnothing,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{pa}_{D_B}(1)=\{3,4\}. \tag{41}
\]
Thus the parent-set alternative of the cited criterion fails.  Under its prescribed reweighted-ancestral construction, the relevant ancestral graph for \(D_A\) has vertex set \(\{1,2,3\}\) and arrows \(1\to3\leftarrow2\), whereas (40) makes the corresponding graph for \(D_B\) the singleton graph on \(\{3\}\).  Graphs on different vertex sets cannot be Markov equivalent, so the reweighted-graph alternative also fails.  Consequently the Teh--Sadeghi--Soo sufficient conditions are not satisfied.

By \(\mathrm{prop{:}four\text{-}node\text{-}cross\text{-}mec\text{-}witness}\),
\[
 p_\star\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I_\star}^{\circ}\cap\mathbb Q^{16},
 \qquad
 T_{D_A,+1}(p_\star)=\frac{13}{20}\neq
 \frac12=T_{D_B,+1}(p_\star). \tag{42}
\]
The outcome space is binary.  If the algorithm's omitted normalization coordinate is \(+1\), then (42) and normalization imply
\[
 T_{D_A,-1}(p_\star)-T_{D_B,-1}(p_\star)
 =-\left\{T_{D_A,+1}(p_\star)-T_{D_B,+1}(p_\star)\right\}\neq0. \tag{43}
\]
If the omitted coordinate is \(-1\), take the tested coordinate \(+1\) directly.  Thus, for the unique tested cell \(y_{\mathrm{test}}\), the positive recorded denominators and \(\mathrm{def{:}pairwise\text{-}cross\text{-}signature}\) give
\[
 F_{D_A,D_B,y_{\mathrm{test}}}(p_\star)
 =B_{D_A,y_{\mathrm{test}}}(p_\star)
  B_{D_B,y_{\mathrm{test}}}(p_\star)
 \left\{T_{D_A,y_{\mathrm{test}}}(p_\star)
       -T_{D_B,y_{\mathrm{test}}}(p_\star)\right\}
 \neq0. \tag{44}
\]
If the corresponding fixed-order normal form were zero, \(\mathrm{lem{:}pairwise\text{-}zero\text{-}normal\text{-}form\text{-}soundness}\) would force equality of that coordinate throughout the exact-oracle model, contradicting (44).  Hence \(\mathrm{def{:}sparse\text{-}simid}\) reaches its exact retained-sample check for this pair and coordinate.  Exact evaluation in (44) succeeds, so it returns \(p_\star\) itself as a rational strictly positive separator.  Its graphwise \(+1\) values remain the two values in (42).  Equations (40)--(41) place the input outside the cited sufficient graphical region, while (42)--(44) give a checkable ambiguity output.  This proves the asserted strict improvement in decision-output coverage.

Fix the accepted input \(\mathfrak u\), its equality-branch circuit \(\tau\), and \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}oracle\text{-}model}\),
\[
 P_z>0\qquad(z\in\Omega). \tag{45}
\]
Every factor recorded in a denominator \(B_{D,y}\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}truncated\text{-}functional}\) is an observed marginal probability, hence a nonempty sum of cells in (45).  Therefore
\[
 B_{D,y}(P)>0\qquad(D\in\mathfrak D,\ y). \tag{46}
\]
There are finitely many such pairs.  Polynomial continuity gives an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(P\) on which all denominators in (46) remain positive.  Every coordinate of \(\tau\) is a quotient of polynomials with nonvanishing denominator on \(U\); hence \(\tau\) is continuously differentiable on \(U\), with derivative \(J_\tau\).

Let \(m=|\Omega|\), let \(e_z\in\mathbb R^m\) be the coordinate vector of cell \(z\), and define \(W_i=e_{Z_i}-P\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}iid\text{-}multinomial}\) and the definition of \(\widehat p_n\) give
\[
 \mathbb E_PW_i=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P(W_iW_i^{\mathsf T})
 =\operatorname{diag}(P)-PP^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma_P,
\]
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat p_n-P)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nW_i. \tag{47}
\]
The \(W_i\) have finite support, so \(\mathbb E_P\|W_i\|^2<\infty\).  Applying \(\mathrm{lem{:}multivariate\text{-}iid\text{-}clt}\) to (47) yields
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat p_n-P)
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_P), \tag{48}
\]
with singular \(\Sigma_P\) allowed.  Moreover,
\[
 \mathbb E_P\|\widehat p_n-P\|_2^2
 =\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_P)}{n}\longrightarrow0, \tag{49}
\]
so \(\widehat p_n\to P\) in probability.  Since \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(P\),
\[
 \Pr_P(\widehat p_n\in U)\longrightarrow1. \tag{50}
\]
By the construction of \(U\), (50) implies that the denominator event in \(\mathrm{def{:}plugin\text{-}estimator}\) has probability tending to one.

Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}multivariate\text{-}delta\text{-}method}\) to (48) and \(\tau\).  Differentiability gives
\[
 \tau(P+h)=\tau(P)+J_\tau(P)h+r(h),
 \qquad
 \frac{\|r(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0. \tag{51}
\]
Equation (48) implies \(\sqrt n\|\widehat p_n-P\|=O_P(1)\); equations (49)--(51) therefore imply \(\sqrt n r(\widehat p_n-P)=o_P(1)\) on the event in (50).  On that event \(\widehat\tau_n=\tau(\widehat p_n)\), while the stipulated off-event value has asymptotically vanishing probability.  Consequently
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\tau_n-\tau(P)\}
 =J_\tau(P)\sqrt n(\widehat p_n-P)+o_P(1)
 \Rightarrow
 \mathcal N\!\left(0,
 J_\tau(P)\Sigma_PJ_\tau(P)^{\mathsf T}\right). \tag{52}
\]

The maps
\[
 p\longmapsto\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 p\longmapsto J_\tau(p) \tag{53}
\]
are continuous at \(P\), the second by continuous differentiability on \(U\).  From (49)--(50),
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_n\xrightarrow{P}\Sigma_P,
 \qquad
 J_\tau(\widehat p_n)\xrightarrow{P}J_\tau(P). \tag{54}
\]
Continuity of matrix multiplication, with the complement of the denominator event again having probability tending to zero, yields
\[
 \widehat V_n\xrightarrow{P}
 J_\tau(P)\Sigma_PJ_\tau(P)^{\mathsf T}. \tag{55}
\]

The circuit fixed in the theorem is the representative circuit on a one-class equality output.  By \(\mathrm{thm{:}sparse\text{-}simid\text{-}completeness}\), for every represented graph and outcome cell,
\[
 \tau_y(P)=T_{D,y}(P)=P_x^D(Y=y), \tag{56}
\]
where the last equality is the theorem's SCM conclusion through the declared DAG intervention functional.  In the zero-normal-form fast branch the same conclusion is also supplied directly by \(\mathrm{lem{:}equality\text{-}branch\text{-}soundness}\).  Thus the center in (52) is the common causal intervention probability, rather than a quantity defined to be causal.

Finally fix the stated cell \(y\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}nondegenerate\text{-}cell}\) is exactly
\[
 \sigma_y^2=e_y^{\mathsf T}J_\tau(P)\Sigma_P
 J_\tau(P)^{\mathsf T}e_y>0. \tag{57}
\]
The scalar marginal of (52), together with (55)--(57), gives
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\tau_{n,y}-P_x(Y=y)\}
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\sigma_y^2),
 \qquad
 \widehat V_{n,yy}\xrightarrow{P}\sigma_y^2. \tag{58}
\]
In particular \(\widehat V_{n,yy}>0\) with probability tending to one.  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}slutsky\text{-}scalar}\),
\[
 \frac{\sqrt n\{\widehat\tau_{n,y}-P_x(Y=y)\}}
      {\sqrt{\widehat V_{n,yy}}}
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,1). \tag{59}
\]
The limiting normal law assigns zero mass to \(\pm1.96\), so (59) proves that the stated Wald interval has limiting coverage
\[
 \Pr\{-1.96\leq Z\leq1.96\}
 =2\Phi(1.96)-1
 =0.9500042097\ldots,
 \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1). \tag{60}
\]
This proves all assertions.

Fix an accepted \(\mathfrak u\), a table \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\), a graph \(D\in\mathfrak D\), and an outcome cell \(y\).  Put \(L=J_{\mathcal I}:s^{\infty}\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}oracle\text{-}model}\), normalization and every oracle-one generator vanish at \(p\), so
\[
 h(p)=0\qquad(h\in J_{\mathcal I}). \tag{61}
\]
The same definition gives \(p_z>0\) for every cell.  Each factor recorded in any \(B_{D',y'}\) is, by \(\mathrm{def{:}truncated\text{-}functional}\), a nonempty observed marginal and hence a nonempty sum of positive cells.  Consequently
\[
 B_{D',y'}(p)>0\quad(D'\in\mathfrak D,\ y'),
 \qquad s(p)\neq0. \tag{62}
\]
If \(h\in L\), saturation supplies \(N\geq0\) such that \(s^Nh\in J_{\mathcal I}\).  Equations (61)--(62) imply \(s(p)^Nh(p)=0\), and division by the nonzero number \(s(p)^N\) gives \(h(p)=0\).  Thus \(p\) lies in the real variety of \(L\).

The hypothesis gives
\[
 \operatorname{NF}_{\prec,K_{\mathcal I}}(F_{D,y})=0. \tag{63}
\]
Reduction by a canonical reduced basis makes (63) equivalent to \(F_{D,y}\in K_{\mathcal I}\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}saturated\text{-}real\text{-}radical}\), \(K_{\mathcal I}=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{L}\) is the ideal of rational polynomials vanishing on the real variety of \(L\).  Hence
\[
 F_{D,y}(p)=0. \tag{64}
\]
Using \(\mathrm{def{:}cross\text{-}signature}\) and the positive denominators in (62), equation (64) is equivalent to
\[
 \frac{A_{D,y}(p)}{B_{D,y}(p)}
 =\frac{A_{D_0,y}(p)}{B_{D_0,y}(p)},
\]
and \(\mathrm{def{:}truncated\text{-}functional}\) therefore gives
\[
 T_{D,y}(p)=T_{D_0,y}(p). \tag{65}
\]
The choices of \(p,D,y\) were arbitrary, proving the asserted equality throughout the exact-oracle model.

By \(\mathrm{lem{:}common\text{-}law\text{-}redundancy}\), the table \(p\) is Markov to every represented DAG.  Applying \(\mathrm{lem{:}dag\text{-}intervention\text{-}functional}\) separately to \(D\) and \(D_0\) proves
\[
 T_{D,y}(p)=P_x^D(Y=y),
 \qquad
 T_{D_0,y}(p)=P_x^{D_0}(Y=y). \tag{66}
\]
Thus (65) identifies \(\tau(p)=(T_{D_0,y}(p))_y\) as the common represented-DAG intervention law; causality is supplied by (66), not by definition.

Finally, \(\mathrm{lem{:}certificate\text{-}size}\) supplies, for each zero normal form in (63), a finite real-Nullstellensatz and saturation identity over a finite real algebraic extension of \(\mathbb Q\), with exact verification polynomial in its total expanded length.  Therefore every equality asserted by the branch carries the required finite checkable certificate.

The first assertion is the maximality conclusion of \(\mathrm{thm{:}sparse\text{-}simid\text{-}completeness}\): its equivalence relation identifies two DAGs exactly when their full intervention vectors agree at every table in \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\), and every partition supporting one common functional per block refines that quotient.

For the specialization, suppose \(\mathfrak D=[G]\), and let \(D,D'\in[G]\) be assigned the same functional by the within-MPDAG enumeration in \(\mathrm{lem{:}guo\text{-}perkovic\text{-}within\text{-}mpdag\text{-}enumeration}\).  The guarantee of that cited result says that their intervention functionals agree for every strictly positive law in the Markov model \(\mathcal P_G^+\).  The assumed inclusion \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal P_G^+\) therefore gives, for every \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\) and every outcome cell \(y\),
\[
 T_{D,y}(p)=T_{D',y}(p). \tag{67}
\]
By the defining equivalence relation of Theorem 2, (67) implies \(D\sim D'\).  Hence each Guo--Perkovic functional class is contained in one SparseSIM-ID class.

The reverse implication would require equality on the restricted set \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\) to imply equality on all of \(\mathcal P_G^+\).  The only assumed relation between these domains is the one-way inclusion, which does not imply that converse.  Accordingly no reverse containment or extensional equality is claimed.

proposed.statement: For \(V=\{1,2,3,4\}\) with binary \(\{-1,+1\}\) states, the tuple \(\mathfrak u_{\star}\) is accepted by \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\text{-}input}\). The table \(p_{\star}\) has exactly the elementary CIs \(1\perp2\), \(1\perp2\mid\{3,4\}\), \(3\perp4\), and \(3\perp4\mid\{1,2\}\). Among all \(543\) labelled DAGs, exactly \(50\) are I-maps, and the unique four-edge minima are \(D_A\) and \(D_B\), which lie in distinct MECs. Their probabilities for \(Y_3=+1\) under \(do(Y_1=+1)\) are \(13/20\) and \(1/2\), respectively.
proposed.justification: The finite instance proves that the target family is nonvacuous beyond one Markov equivalence class.
proposed.gap: The examples in Teh, Sadeghi, and Soo motivate tied sparsest outputs but do not provide this binary rational exact-oracle enumeration certificate.
proposed.consumer: Implementers obtain a unit test whose graph counts, oracle bits, and intervention gap are all checkable by exact arithmetic.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The causal interpretation of the computed truncated factors uses the declared DAG intervention-functional lemma, so that dependency must be explicit.

proposed.statement: Corollary 1 (strictness relative to Teh--Sadeghi--Soo). For the certified input \(\mathfrak u_{\star}\) and query \(P_{Y_1=+1}(Y_3=+1)\), the sufficient graphical conditions of Theorem 3.2 of Teh, Sadeghi, and Soo are not satisfied, whereas \(\operatorname{SparseSIM\text{-}ID}\) returns a rational positive separator; the table \(p_{\star}\) is an explicit admissible separator with graphwise values \(13/20\) under \(D_A\) and \(1/2\) under \(D_B\). Hence SparseSIM-ID strictly tightens that sufficient-only test on certified tied-sparsest inputs by resolving at least one query on which it is undecided.
proposed.justification: This finite corollary turns the comparator relation into an auditable strict inclusion rather than a prose promise.
proposed.gap: Teh, Sadeghi, and Soo give a sufficient graphical criterion and leave necessity unresolved; this certified exact-oracle instance is outside their decided region but receives a checkable nonidentification certificate.
proposed.consumer: A regression test for Tetrad SP and causaldag or GSP can verify that an undecided graphical case is reported as exact ambiguity rather than silently selecting a graph.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Soundly skipping a separator decision after a zero pairwise normal form uses the declared pairwise normal-form soundness lemma and the pairwise signature definition.

proposed.statement:
For every finite input \(\mathfrak u\) accepted by \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\text{-}input}\), if
\[
 \operatorname{NF}_{\prec,K_{\mathcal I}}(F_{D,y})=0
 \quad\text{for every }D\in\mathfrak D\text{ and every outcome cell }y,
\]
then the equality output of \(\operatorname{SparseSIM\text{-}ID}\) is sound: for every \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\),
\[
 T_{D,y}(p)=T_{D_0,y}(p)
 \quad\text{for every }D\in\mathfrak D\text{ and }y.
\]
Thus \(\tau(p)=(T_{D_0,y}(p))_y\) is the common represented-DAG intervention law, and each asserted equality has a finite exactly checkable real-Nullstellensatz and saturation certificate.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The statement concludes equality of causal intervention laws, so its proof must explicitly depend on the theorem connecting truncated factors to Markovian SCM interventions.

proposed.statement: Theorem 3 (fixed-input plug-in inference). Fix one finite input \(\mathfrak u\) accepted by \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\text{-}input}\), fix its equality-branch circuit \(\tau\), and fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\). Every recorded denominator is positive at \(P\), so the rational circuit \(\tau\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(P\), the event defining \(\widehat\tau_n\) has probability tending to one, and \(\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau(P))\Rightarrow\mathcal N\left(0,J_{\tau}(P)\Sigma_PJ_{\tau}(P)^{\mathsf T}\right)\). Moreover, \(\widehat V_n\xrightarrow{P}J_{\tau}(P)\Sigma_PJ_{\tau}(P)^{\mathsf T}\). If \(\sigma_y^2>0\), then \(\widehat\tau_{n,y}\pm1.96\sqrt{\widehat V_{n,yy}/n}\) has limiting coverage \(0.9500042097\ldots\) for \(P_x(Y=y)\).
proposed.justification: A certified population functional should produce standard sampling inference without graphwise duplicate estimates.
proposed.gap: Chang, Guo, and Malinsky handle data-driven graph selection by interval unions; this theorem instead gives pointwise plug-in inference for one fixed certified oracle, tied family, and arithmetic circuit.
proposed.consumer: After a population or externally certified discovery analysis, practitioners can estimate the common intervention probability with one covariance calculation.

proposed_core_edits.reason: A one-class equality output may be certified semialgebraically even when a normal form is nonzero, so the plug-in theorem must depend on the full quotient theorem for its causal center.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an input \(\mathfrak u\) accepted by \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\text{-}input}\), a graph \(D\in\mathfrak D\), and an outcome cell \(y\).  For each conditional-independence statement \(c\) with \(\mathcal I(c)=0\), set
\[
 h_c(p)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal C_0(\mathcal I,c)}g(p)^2,
\]
as in the statement, and define finite subsets of \(\mathbb Q[p_z:z\in\Omega]\) by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E&=\mathcal C_1(\mathcal I)\cup
 \left\{\sum_{z\in\Omega}p_z-1\right\},\\
 G&=\{p_z:z\in\Omega\}\cup
 \{h_c:\mathcal I(c)=0\},\\
 H&=\{p_z:z\in\Omega\}\cup
 \{h_c:\mathcal I(c)=0\}\cup\{F_{D,y}\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
These sets are finite because \(V\), every \(\Omega_v\), and hence \(\Omega\), are finite by \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\text{-}input}\), and the collection of conditional-independence statements on the finite set \(V\) is finite.  Their coefficients are rational: the conditional-independence minors have integer coefficients by the determinantal construction of \(\mathcal C_1(\mathcal I)\) and \(\mathcal C_0(\mathcal I,c)\), normalization has integer coefficients, each \(h_c\) is a sum of squares of such minors, and \(F_{D,y}\) is an integer polynomial by \(\mathrm{def{:}cross\text{-}signature}\).

Use the notation \(S(E,G,H)\) from \(\mathrm{lem{:}semialgebraic\text{-}decision\text{-}with\text{-}certificates}\).  For each cell \(z\), the two requirements \(p_z\geq0\) from \(G\) and \(p_z\neq0\) from \(H\) are equivalent over \(\mathbb R\) to \(p_z>0\).  For every bit-zero statement \(c\), the definition of \(h_c\) gives \(h_c(p)\geq0\) for every real \(p\), and the requirements \(h_c(p)\geq0\) and \(h_c(p)\neq0\) are therefore equivalent to \(h_c(p)>0\).  The equality requirements indexed by \(E\) are precisely normalization and all bit-one oracle equalities.  Finally, the remaining inequation indexed by \(H\) is \(F_{D,y}(p)\neq0\).  Thus \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}oracle\text{-}model}\) yields the exact set identity
\[
 S(E,G,H)
 =\left\{p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}:F_{D,y}(p)\neq0\right\}.
\tag{1}
\]

Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}semialgebraic\text{-}decision\text{-}with\text{-}certificates}\) with \(k=|\Omega|\).  Its algorithm terminates after finitely many exact algebraic-number operations and decides whether the set in \((1)\) is empty.  The nonempty and empty cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so exactly one branch is returned.

Suppose first that \(S(E,G,H)\neq\varnothing\).  The cited decision lemma returns a point, represented by a rational univariate representation together with coordinate minimal polynomials and rational isolating or Thom data, satisfying
\[
 p^\dagger\in S(E,G,H)\cap\mathbb R_{\mathrm{alg}}^\Omega.
\]
By \((1)\),
\[
 p^\dagger\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\cap
 \mathbb R_{\mathrm{alg}}^\Omega
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 F_{D,y}(p^\dagger)\neq0.
\tag{2}
\]
Every observed-table marginal that occurs as a denominator factor in the truncated factorization is a sum over a nonempty set of cells.  Strict positivity in \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\), used in \((2)\), makes each such marginal strictly positive.  After the cancellations prescribed by \(\mathrm{def{:}truncated\text{-}functional}\), the recorded denominators are products of the remaining positive marginal factors; hence
\[
 B_{D,y}(p^\dagger)>0
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 B_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)>0.
\tag{3}
\]
Using \(T_{D,y}=A_{D,y}/B_{D,y}\) from \(\mathrm{def{:}truncated\text{-}functional}\), the definition of \(F_{D,y}\) in \(\mathrm{def{:}cross\text{-}signature}\), and the legitimate divisions ensured by \((3)\), we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 T_{D,y}(p^\dagger)-T_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)
 &=\frac{A_{D,y}(p^\dagger)}{B_{D,y}(p^\dagger)}
   -\frac{A_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)}{B_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)}\\
 &=\frac{A_{D,y}(p^\dagger)B_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)
          -A_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)B_{D,y}(p^\dagger)}
         {B_{D,y}(p^\dagger)B_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)}\\
 &=\frac{F_{D,y}(p^\dagger)}
         {B_{D,y}(p^\dagger)B_{D_0,y}(p^\dagger)}\neq0,
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality follows from \((2)\) and \((3)\).  This is the required exact real-algebraic positive-chamber separator, and all parts of its encoding are checkable by the exact arithmetic guaranteed by the cited decision lemma.

Suppose instead that \(S(E,G,H)=\varnothing\).  The same decision lemma returns a finite Positivstellensatz identity
\[
 a_0+b_0+c_0^2=0,
 \qquad
 a_0\in\langle E\rangle,
 \quad b_0\in\operatorname{PO}(G),
 \quad c_0\in\operatorname{Mon}(H),
\tag{4}
\]
over a finite real algebraic extension of \(\mathbb Q\).  Identity \((4)\) is a finite, exactly checkable infeasibility certificate for \(S(E,G,H)\).  By \((1)\), its infeasibility conclusion is equivalent to
\[
 F_{D,y}(p)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}.
\tag{5}
\]
Fix any \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\).  Repeating the denominator argument leading to \((3)\) gives
\[
 B_{D,y}(p)B_{D_0,y}(p)>0.
\tag{6}
\]
Equations \((5)\) and \((6)\), together with the same cross-multiplication identity, imply
\[
 T_{D,y}(p)-T_{D_0,y}(p)
 =\frac{F_{D,y}(p)}{B_{D,y}(p)B_{D_0,y}(p)}=0.
\]
Since \(p\) was arbitrary, universal equality holds throughout \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\).  Conversely, if the two functionals differ at some \(p\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal I}^{\circ}\), positivity of their denominators as in \((6)\) forces \(F_{D,y}(p)\neq0\), and then \((1)\) makes \(S(E,G,H)\) nonempty.  Therefore feasibility is exactly the positive exact-oracle separation criterion, while infeasibility is exactly universal equality on that chamber.  The argument nowhere infers positive-chamber feasibility from saturated-real-radical nonmembership.
